## References

1. [HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17354)

# Notes

## The problem: benchmarks that don't *mean* anything

Suppose you read "Claude 3.7 scores 71% on benchmark X." So what? Is that good? Does it mean the model can do a junior engineer's job? Replace a security analyst? Most AI benchmarks are **ungrounded**: the score is a number on an arbitrary scale (% of MMLU questions, ELO on some leaderboard) with no direct line to anything we care about in the real world. If we want to *predict the societal impact* of increasingly autonomous AI agents — automation of jobs, acceleration of R&D, ability to run multi-step cyber operations — we need a benchmark whose metric is **grounded**: it connects model performance to a real-world quantity.

HCAST (Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks), from **METR** (Model Evaluation & Threat Research), is METR's answer. The grounding quantity is deceptively simple: **how long does this task take a skilled human?** If you know that, then "the model succeeds at 70% of tasks that take humans under an hour, but under 20% of tasks that take humans 4+ hours" is a statement you can actually reason about. You've converted an abstract success rate into a *human-time horizon* — a far more interpretable axis than "points."

This note decodes HCAST itself (the 189-task benchmark + the human-baselining machinery). HCAST is the foundational task suite under METR's much more famous follow-up, "Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks" ([2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)), which fit a curve to these human times and announced the "**AI time horizons double every ~7 months**" result. HCAST is the ruler; that paper is the measurement.

## The core idea, simply

Build a suite of *agentic software tasks*. For each task:

1. Put a **skilled human** in *exactly* the same sandboxed environment an AI agent would get — same instructions, same files, same SSH terminal, same containerized machine. Time how long they take to solve it. This is the **human baseline**.
2. Put **AI agents** (with a scaffold that lets them run Bash/Python) in that same environment and measure their success rate.
3. Now you can plot **agent success rate vs. human completion time**. The x-axis is grounded in human labor.

The conceptual leap: difficulty is no longer "hard/medium/easy" or "% of a test." Difficulty is *measured in hours of expert human work*, and you can ask the killer question — **"what's the longest (in human-time) task an agent can reliably do?"**

## What's in the benchmark

**189 tasks**, grouped into **78 families** (1–5 tasks each; a family shares structure/code, e.g. several instances of the same crypto-cracking challenge with different parameters). Four domains:

- **General reasoning — 89 tasks.** Common-sense, algorithmic, logical, statistical puzzles. The "broad" base.
- **Cybersecurity — 39 tasks.** CTF-style: cryptography, reverse engineering, exploit development.
- **Software engineering (SWE) — 31 tasks.** Feature implementation, algorithmic optimization, debugging, DevOps.
- **Machine learning engineering (MLE) — 30 tasks.** Training/finetuning, data science, model debugging, building scaffolding. These are the *longest and hardest* to baseline.

**Task structure.** Each task is a self-contained unit with:
- **Initial information / instructions** (what to do),
- **A containerized environment** with setup code (the agent or human gets SSH access to an identical box — some tasks need GPUs, external VMs, or API access),
- **An algorithmic scoring function** — mostly **binary** pass/fail, some **continuous** with a defined target threshold.

Tasks span **~1 minute to 8+ hours** of human time (the broader METR suite extends this to ~30 hours by adding RE-Bench's 8-hour ML-research tasks). The automatic, code-based scoring is the design constraint that makes large-scale agent evaluation possible — no human in the grading loop.

**Provenance.** 143 tasks built in-house by METR staff/contractors; 46 acquired via an **external bounty program** for diversity. 11 example families are public at `github.com/METR/hcast-public`; the other 178 are **withheld to prevent training contamination and benchmark hill-climbing**. The paper ships a **canary string** (`hcast:5a51:26b5c67b-...`) asking labs to exclude it from training corpora — a recurring move in eval papers to detect/avoid memorization.

## The hard part: collecting human baselines

This is where the paper's real cost lives, and where it differs from every "throw a test at the model" benchmark.

**The baseliners.** ~140 skilled professionals — typically top-100-university degrees or 3+ years of relevant experience. For ML/SWE/cyber, they had to pass **domain qualification tasks** first. Recruited largely through METR's networks.

**The conditions (the whole point is *identical* to the agent).** Same task environment via SSH, same instructions, same resources. They were given **limited web access** — to avoid penalizing them for "unrealistic hindrances" like forgetting syntax (the agent has equivalent knowledge baked into its weights), but **forbidden from using AI assistants or Wolfram Alpha** (that would defeat the human-baseline purpose). Sessions were **screen-recorded via Loom** for QA.

**The incentive design (a subtle but important detail).** Naive hourly pay incentivizes *slow* work; naive piece-rate incentivizes *sloppy* work. HCAST uses a composite:
- Base rate **$50–$100/hr**,
- A **completion bonus** ≈ (r/2)·t where r = hourly rate and t = average task time,
- A **speed bonus** ≈ r·t for beating other baseliners' time on the same task.

The goal: reward *successfully* finishing without rewarding endless gold-plating/verification — i.e., approximate how a competent professional actually works. This is a genuine measurement-design contribution, not just a benchmark dump.

**The numbers.** **563 baseline attempts** across 139 of the 189 tasks, **>1,500 hours** of expert work. **341 succeeded** → a **61% baseline success rate**. 110 tasks got ≥1 successful baseline; **50 tasks have no baseline at all** and **29 had only failed attempts**. For the **79 tasks without a successful baseline, researcher forecasts** were used instead.

**Turning attempts into a time estimate.** For a task with ≥1 successful baseline, the human time is the **geometric mean of successful baseline times** (geometric, because completion times are roughly log-normal — they span orders of magnitude, so you average in log-space). For the rest, researcher forecasts fill in. How good are those forecasts? They correlate with actual baselines at **R² ≈ 0.51**, and the paper notes the informal estimates track reality but **systematically underestimate the hard tasks** — a known honest weakness.

**Resulting difficulty distribution (by human time):**
- < 15 min: **41 tasks**
- 15 min – 1 hr: **59 tasks**
- 1 – 4 hr: **57 tasks**
- > 4 hr: **32 tasks**

**Domain baseline coverage is uneven** (and revealing): SWE 80% of tasks have a successful baseline, cyber 69%, general reasoning 56%, **MLE only 37%** — MLE tasks are the longest and hardest, so even skilled humans frequently failed to baseline them in the allotted budget. This is a quiet signal that the upper end of the benchmark is genuinely hard.

## Quality assurance (why you should believe the scores)

Eval papers live or die on whether the scoring can be gamed. HCAST's pipeline:
1. **Blind human QA** — testers not involved in authoring run tasks to surface bugs/ambiguities.
2. **Gold reference solutions** implemented where feasible.
3. **AI-agent QA at scale** — Claude 3.5 Sonnet attempted *every* task **5×** → **945 transcripts**, all **manually reviewed** to confirm legitimate solves and, crucially, to **catch reward hacking** (agents finding a shortcut the scorer wrongly accepts).
4. **Baseline QC** — manual review of the majority of successful baselines, prioritizing anomalies, using the Loom recordings.

They also label tasks on two axes that matter for interpreting results:
- **Expertise required:** no-experience 15.4% of families, <1yr 35.9%, 1–3yr 38.5%, >3yr 10.3%.
- **Contamination risk:** private-solution+private-problem **67.9%** (hard to memorize), public-but-hard-to-memorize 16.7%, **easy-to-memorize 15.4%**. So ~2/3 of the suite is contamination-resistant by construction.

## How agents are evaluated

**Models × scaffolds tested:** GPT-4o (Modular scaffold), OpenAI **o1** (Triframe), **Claude 3.5 Sonnet** 20241022 (Modular), **Claude 3.7 Sonnet** extended-thinking (Triframe).

**Scaffolds** (both are ReAct-style — interleave reasoning and tool actions; tools = Python execution + Bash):
- **Modular** — one command per iteration, with chain-of-thought planning. Simple loop.
- **Triframe** — a best-of-sampling controller: it generates **1 plan**, then **3 plan-aligned** + **3 plan-agnostic** candidate commands, **scores all six** on a −2…+2 scale, and executes the best. More compute per step, more robust to a single bad action.

**Resource limits:** **10 hours wall-clock**, **2M tokens** (Modular) / **8M tokens** (Triframe). **≥5 runs per agent per task** (3 tasks had only 2–4). An "action" = one Python/Bash execution, *excluding* internal reasoning.

## The headline results

Success rate degrades **predictably and steeply** with human task length — this monotonic, smooth degradation is exactly what makes the time-horizon framing work:

- **< 15 min human tasks:** ~**70–80%** agent success (Claude 3.7, o1 highest)
- **15 min – 1 hr:** ~**60–70%**
- **1 – 4 hr:** ~**30–40%**
- **> 4 hr:** **< 20%**

The cliff sits between the 1-hour and 4-hour buckets. **Claude 3.7 Sonnet and o1 lead at every difficulty level** — the two *reasoning-heavy* models — suggesting extended reasoning/test-time compute is the differentiator on the long tail (cf. [[PPO vs GRPO - Policy Optimization for Alignment]] and [[Reinforcement Learning - Foundations, MDPs, and Control Algorithms]] for the RL/reasoning training that produces these models).

**Effort profile:** for ~1/3 of tasks, successful runs took a **median of 5–15 actions**; ~10% of tasks needed a median **>25 actions**. So solving the harder tasks is genuinely multi-step agentic work, not one-shot Q&A.

## How the grounding becomes a number (the bridge to time-horizons)

HCAST per se reports the bucketed success rates above. Its sibling paper turns them into a single scalar via a **logistic regression**: model success probability as a function of **log(human completion time)**:

P(success) = σ( a + b · log(human_time) ), with b < 0.

The **50%-task-completion time horizon** is the human time at which this curve crosses 50% — i.e., solve for log(human_time) = −a/b. Intuition: "the duration of human work at which the model is a coin-flip to succeed." Using log-time matters because difficulty scales multiplicatively (a 2-hr task isn't "1 hr harder" than a 1-hr task, it's *twice* as long) — the log makes the relationship linear and the regression well-behaved.

Plugged into HCAST + RE-Bench + 66 short tasks (SWAA), this gave the famous results: **Claude 3.7 Sonnet ≈ 59-minute 50% time horizon**, with the horizon **doubling roughly every 7 months since 2019** (and possibly accelerating to ~4 months in 2024–25). Crucially, the **80%** threshold doubling time (213 days) is nearly identical to the **50%** one (212 days) — so the *trend* is robust to the threshold — even though the *level* gap is large (Claude 3.7: ~59 min at 50% reliability but only ~15 min at 80%). For binarizing HCAST runs, the threshold is the same target score the human baseliner aimed for. (Sources: [METR blog](https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/), [arXiv 2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499), [METR time-horizons](https://metr.org/time-horizons/).)

## Why agents fail (qualitative)

The failure modes are characteristically *agentic*, not knowledge gaps:
1. **Premature abandonment** — submitting a known-wrong answer while still having compute/tokens left. (The agent "gives up.")
2. **Poor error recovery** — doubling down on a failing approach instead of pivoting. No metacognition about being stuck.
3. **Bad resource management** — fumbling token/time budget under constraint.
4. **Low-feedback environments** — markedly worse on blackbox optimization (mean scores ~0.21–0.26), where the environment gives little signal to learn from.

These are *control/agency* failures — exactly the behaviors safety work tries to study and constrain. An agent that can't recover from errors or manage a budget over a 4-hour horizon is also one whose autonomy is, for now, self-limiting.

## Genuine limitations (the authors are candid)

- **Realism gap.** Tasks have clean, well-defined scope and *automatic* scoring. Real economically-valuable work is ambiguous, requires subjective judgment, and involves collaborating with people. HCAST tasks are **solitary** and **objectively gradable** — that's a measurement convenience, not the real world.
- **Baseline interpretation is fuzzy.** Baseliners often have *limited prior experience* with the specific task → learning-time overhead inflates times; expertise-task matching is imperfect; the **61% baseline success rate** can't be directly compared to agent success rates (different incentives, baseliners may quit when an agent wouldn't). The geometric-mean-of-successes estimator also ignores how often humans *fail*.
- **Forecast reliance.** 79/189 tasks use researcher *forecasts* (R²≈0.51 vs. actuals, underestimating hard tasks) rather than measured human times — noise in exactly the long-horizon regime that matters most.
- **Web access asymmetry.** Humans got limited web access; agents rely on memorized equivalents — not a perfectly matched condition.
- **Cost & scale.** GPU/VM/API infra is expensive; **1,500+ hours** of expert baselining is slow and costly — limiting how fast the suite can grow or be re-baselined.

## Where it sits vs. prior work, and why it matters for safety

Most agentic benchmarks (SWE-bench, CTF suites, MLE-bench) measure *capability on a fixed task distribution* with no human-time grounding. HCAST's contribution is the **calibration layer** — the painstaking human baselines that let any agent score be read as a *human-time horizon*. That's the difference between "the model scores 50%" and "the model can autonomously do tasks that take a human ~an hour."

For AI safety / dangerous-capability evaluation, this grounding is the load-bearing piece. METR's mandate is **pre-deployment dangerous-capability evals** (it informed evaluations of GPT-4.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3). Knowing the human-time horizon of an agent's autonomy is the prerequisite for any **AI-control** argument: control protocols assume you've bounded what a model can actually accomplish before a human catches it. HCAST is what supplies that bound empirically. The "<20% past 4 hours" result is reassuring *today* (frontier agents can't yet sustain long autonomous operations), but the **7-month doubling** is the alarming trend line — it forecasts agents capable of day- and week-long tasks within a few years, which is precisely the regime where untrusted-model control becomes essential (see [[Shlegeris Greenblatt - The Case for Ensuring Powerful AIs are Controlled]], [[AI Control - Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion]], and the resampling-based monitoring in [[Ctrl-Z - Controlling AI Agents via Resampling]]). The failure modes HCAST surfaces — premature abandonment, no error recovery, budget mismanagement — are the *current* ceilings on autonomy; the safety question is what happens when training closes them.

In one line: **HCAST is the human-calibrated yardstick that turns agentic-AI scores into "hours of expert work the agent can do unsupervised" — the unit that dangerous-capability forecasting and AI-control arguments actually need.**
